stem_html:
The collection of letters, ledgers, and shipping manifests that the archivists recovered from the flooded basement of the customs house ______ the only surviving record of the port's trade in the decade before the fire.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Twenty-two words of interference. Between the subject and the verb sit three plural nouns and a relative clause with its own plural verb. Every one of them pulls the ear toward a plural verb.
  • The nearest noun is never the subject here. “Customs house” is singular and “manifests” is plural; neither is what the verb agrees with.
  • Two wrong choices are plural in disguise. “Have constituted” and “are constituting” hide their number in an auxiliary, so a student checking only the main verb misses it.

Why A is wrong Plural. Strip the modifiers and the sentence is “The collection constitute,” which is the error the intervening plurals are there to disguise.

Why B is right The subject is “The collection,” a singular noun; everything from “of letters” to “customs house” modifies it. A singular subject takes “constitutes,” and the simple present is right for a state that still holds.

Why C is wrong Plural agreement again, in an auxiliary. The present perfect also implies a span of time reaching the present that the sentence has no use for.

Why D is wrong Plural, and the progressive says the collection is in the process of becoming the record, which is not a process at all.

stem_html:
By the time the survey team reached the ridge in 1911, the glacier that earlier expeditions had described as reaching the valley floor ______ nearly two kilometers up the mountain.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Three past events, one order. The earlier expeditions described the glacier, then it retreated, then the 1911 team arrived. Only one tense marks the middle event as earlier than the last.
  • The present perfect looks careful. “Has retreated” is the tense students reach for to signal completion, and it anchors the completion to now rather than to 1911.
  • The simple past is not wrong-sounding. Choice D reads acceptably aloud, which is why it is the most chosen distractor; it simply loses the ordering the sentence is built to convey.

Why A is wrong “Would retreat” looks forward from a past point. That reverses the order the sentence establishes and turns a completed retreat into one still to come.

Why B is wrong The present perfect ties the action to the present moment. The reference point here is 1911, stated in the opening clause, so the sentence would claim the retreat is complete as of today.

Why C is right The past perfect places the retreat before the team's arrival, which is what “By the time” demands. It also keeps the three events in order relative to the pluperfect “had described.”

Why D is wrong The simple past puts the retreat on the same footing as the arrival, so the sequence collapses and “already” is left with nothing to be earlier than.

stem_html:
Neither the two conservators who cleaned the panel nor the curator who commissioned the analysis ______ willing to say, before the pigment results arrived, whether the underdrawing was the artist's own.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The proximity rule, not the counting rule. With “neither … nor,” the verb agrees with whichever subject is nearer to it. The nearer one here is “the curator,” singular, even though a plural noun opens the sentence.
  • Two plural nouns are in front. “Conservators” and the number two both push the ear toward a plural verb, which is exactly the trap.
  • Tense as a second trap. The sentence is about a past moment, before the pigment results arrived, so the present-tense choice fails even when its number is right.

Why A is wrong Plural, and the present perfect connects the unwillingness to the present, while the sentence has fixed it at a moment before the results arrived.

Why B is wrong Plural and present tense, wrong on both counts, though it reads smoothly because the plural is what the opening of the sentence has primed.

Why C is wrong Plural, agreeing with the noun furthest from the verb. That is the error the sentence is constructed to invite.

Why D is right “Neither A nor B” takes its number from B, and B is “the curator,” singular. The simple past matches the past reference point the sentence supplies.

stem_html:
Metallurgists have long held that the Damascus blades' pattern comes from the crucible process that produced the steel. A 2006 electron-microscope study did find carbon nanotubes in a surviving blade, which appeared to settle the matter. ______ the same structures have since been produced in ordinary steel simply by repeated heating and quenching, so their presence identifies a treatment rather than a source.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The sentence before the blank agrees with the thesis. Two sentences in a row support the crucible account, so the ear expects a third. The blank is where the passage turns.
  • “Consequently” is the reversal trap. The final clause sounds like a conclusion, so a causal transition feels right, and it makes the new finding follow from the one it contradicts.
  • Additive transitions survive a fast read. “Moreover” is invisible in a hurry, which is why it is chosen when the reader has not registered that the argument has changed direction.

Why A is right The nanotube result appeared to settle the matter; the next sentence removes its force by showing the same structures arise from ordinary heating and quenching. That is a contrast, and only a contrastive transition marks it.

Why B is wrong Exemplifying. The later study is not an instance of the nanotube finding; it is a competing explanation of it.

Why C is wrong Causal. It claims the nanotube finding leads to the conclusion that nanotubes identify a treatment rather than a source, when in fact the later work overturns what the finding seemed to show.

Why D is wrong Additive. It would present the later work as further support for the crucible thesis, and the later work does the reverse.

stem_html:
Economist Dani Chen's model predicts that a city's transit ridership falls when parking is cheap. Ridership in Zurich rose through the 1990s while parking prices there were frozen by ordinance, an outcome the model does not anticipate. ______ Chen argues that the freeze was accompanied by a cap on the number of spaces, so the cost of parking to a driver — time spent searching — rose even as the posted price did not.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The blank sits between an objection and a reply. Naming that relation is the whole task, and three of the four choices name some other relation that is locally plausible.
  • “In other words” is the paraphrase trap. The sentence after the blank does explain something, so a restating transition feels natural — but it restates nothing; it introduces a new fact about the space cap.
  • Concession read as capitulation. “Admittedly” would have Chen conceding the counterexample, and the sentence is where the counterexample is answered.

Why A is wrong Conceding. It would signal that Chen accepts the counterexample as damaging, when the sentence is the argument that it is not.

Why B is right The middle sentence is a counterexample to the model and the last is Chen's rebuttal, which reinterprets the Zurich case rather than accepting it. A transition marking a reply is the only one that fits both.

Why C is wrong Comparative. It would make Chen's argument parallel to the Zurich anomaly rather than a response to it.

Why D is wrong Restating. The final sentence introduces information found nowhere earlier — a cap on the number of spaces — so it cannot be a rewording of what came before.

stem_html:
Restoring a wetland does not simply reverse its draining. The plant community that returns is usually assembled from whatever seed is still viable in the soil or arrives on the wind, which rarely resembles the community that was lost. ______ a restored fen in Cambridgeshire regained its water table within two years but, twenty years on, holds barely a third of the sedge species recorded there in 1900.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A sentence with a “but” inside it looks contrastive. The Cambridgeshire sentence contains its own internal contrast — water back, species not — which tempts a contrastive transition for the relation between sentences.
  • Generalization followed by a case. The relation to name is the one between the claim and the single site that illustrates it, not the one inside the last sentence.

Why A is wrong Causal. A single site does not follow as a consequence of the generalization; it is evidence for it.

Why B is wrong Contrastive. It would set the fen against the claim, but the fen is an instance of the claim: the community that returned does not resemble the one that was lost.

Why C is right The second sentence states a general pattern and the third gives one site that shows it. Exemplification is exactly that relation, and the internal “but” belongs to the example, not to the link.

Why D is wrong Also contrastive, and it invites the reader to look for two things being compared across the sentences when only one case is offered.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2019 article on urban heat.

Planting trees is the intervention that cities reach for first, and it is not wrong. A mature canopy can hold the air beneath it several degrees cooler than an exposed street. But a sapling planted this spring will not shade anyone for fifteen years, and the residents of the hottest blocks are, on the whole, the residents least likely to still be living there in fifteen years. Awnings, painted roofs, and open hydrants are unglamorous by comparison; they also work this July.

Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"It disputes the claim that tree canopy lowers street-level temperatures.","trap":"too-extreme"},{"letter":"B","content":"It provides statistical support for the assertion made in the preceding sentence.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"C","content":"It concedes a drawback of a proposal that the writer nevertheless goes on to endorse.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"It introduces the mismatch in timing that the rest of the text uses to argue for other measures."}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “But” is not always a concession. The sentence opens with a contrast word, so it reads as a grudging admission — and the final sentence shows it was the pivot of the argument, not an aside within it.
  • Function is judged by what follows. The last sentence recommends awnings, painted roofs and open hydrants because they work this July. That is what the underlined sentence exists to set up.
  • Doubting the timeline is not doubting the effect. The writer grants that a mature canopy cools; the objection is entirely about when.

Why A is wrong It disputes nothing about the cooling effect; the preceding sentence's claim about a mature canopy is left standing.

Why B is wrong No statistics appear. “On the whole” is a hedge, not data, and the sentence complicates the previous claim rather than supporting it.

Why C is wrong The writer does not go on to endorse tree planting. The closing sentence recommends the alternatives, so this describes a structure the text does not have.

Why D is right The sentence puts two clocks side by side — fifteen years to shade, and residents unlikely to still be living there in fifteen years — and the text closes by preferring measures that work this July. It is the hinge the conclusion turns on.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2016 essay on museum lighting.

For most of the twentieth century, conservators lit galleries as dimly as visitors would tolerate, on the reasoning that light is cumulative damage and darkness is free. The arithmetic was sound. What it left out was that a painting nobody can see is also a painting nobody comes back to see, and a museum that empties out conserves nothing for long.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "It presents a longstanding practice, grants the reasoning behind it, and then identifies a cost that reasoning omitted."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "It describes a practice, shows that its underlying arithmetic was mistaken, and proposes a replacement.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "It contrasts two schools of conservation and declines to choose between them.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "It traces the history of a technique and predicts its return.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Granting is not refuting. The text says in so many words that the arithmetic was sound. A choice claiming the reasoning was mistaken contradicts a sentence you can point at.
  • A structure question is answered by the whole shape. Any choice that describes only the first half will match the opening and fail at the end.

Why A is right Three moves, in order: the practice of lighting galleries as dimly as visitors would tolerate, the concession that the arithmetic was sound, and then what it left out — that an unvisited museum conserves nothing for long.

Why B is wrong The text explicitly grants the arithmetic. Its objection is that the calculation was incomplete, which is a different charge from being wrong, and no replacement practice is proposed.

Why C is wrong Only one school is described. There is no second position in the text to contrast it with.

Why D is wrong No prediction is made, and the history occupies one clause rather than the structure of the passage.

stem_html:
Researchers testing whether background music affects reading comprehension had participants read passages in silence, with instrumental music, and with music that had lyrics. Comprehension was equally high in silence and with instrumental music, and lower with lyrics. A follow-up used instrumental music at a volume loud enough that participants reported difficulty concentrating, and comprehension fell to the level seen with lyrics. Taken together, these results suggest that the interference is caused not by the presence of music as such but by ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "the participants' expectation that music will be distracting.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "any feature of the audio that competes for attention, whether that is language or loudness."}, {"letter": "C", "content": "the linguistic content of the lyrics specifically.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "the total amount of time participants spent listening to music while reading.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The first study alone gives the wrong answer. Read only the first result and lyrics are the culprit; the whole point of the follow-up is that loud instrumental music does the same damage.
  • The blank is governed by “not … but.” Whatever fills it has to be something other than the mere presence of music, and it has to cover both experiments at once.
  • Expectation is never measured. A plausible psychological story that the passage supplies no evidence for is the standard Inferences distractor.

Why A is wrong Nothing in either study measures what participants expected. The reported difficulty concentrating is an effect of the volume, not evidence about anticipation.

Why B is right Two very different manipulations — lyrics, and instrumental music loud enough to make concentrating hard — did the same damage: in the follow-up, comprehension fell to the level seen with lyrics, while quiet instrumental music cost nothing at all. The common factor is competition for attention, and only this choice names something both conditions share.

Why C is wrong This is the conclusion the first experiment alone supports, and the follow-up rules it out: loud instrumental music has no linguistic content and lowered comprehension just as much.

Why D is wrong Listening time is not varied in either study. All conditions involve reading a passage while the audio plays.

stem_html:
Sediment cores from Lake Suigetsu preserve one varve, or annual layer, per year, and each varve traps a small quantity of leaf material. Radiocarbon dates from those leaves can therefore be checked against a calendar count of the layers. For the interval from 12,000 to 15,000 years ago, the radiocarbon dates run consistently younger than the varve count by up to several centuries, and the size of the gap changes smoothly rather than jumping. This pattern suggests that the discrepancy arises from ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"the difficulty of counting varves in cores older than 15,000 years.","trap":"wrong-part-of-passage"},{"letter":"B","content":"occasional years in which no varve was deposited at all.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"C","content":"gradual variation in the atmospheric concentration of radiocarbon over that interval."},{"letter":"D","content":"contamination of the leaf material by younger carbon during handling.","trap":"out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The word doing the work is “smoothly.” A discrepancy that changes smoothly rather than jumping rules out anything episodic, and two of the wrong choices are episodic.
  • A real laboratory hazard, unmentioned. Contamination is a genuine problem in radiocarbon work, which makes it attractive; nothing in the passage points to it, and it would not vary smoothly with age.
  • The interval is stated, then ignored. Choice A talks about cores older than 15,000 years, which is outside the interval the pattern describes.

Why A is wrong The passage confines the pattern to the interval from 12,000 to 15,000 years ago. Counting difficulties beyond 15,000 years lie outside what is being explained.

Why B is wrong Missing years would make the varve count too young, not too old, and missed layers would show up as irregular jumps rather than a smoothly changing gap.

Why C is right If the amount of radiocarbon in the atmosphere drifted over the period, every sample formed then inherits a slightly wrong apparent age, and the error changes gradually as the concentration does. That matches both the direction and the smoothness of the observed gap.

Why D is wrong Handling contamination is unsystematic. It would produce scattered anomalies, not a gap that changes smoothly across three thousand years, and the passage reports no such handling.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2021 article about the domestication of horses.

Genetic work published that year traced nearly all modern domestic horses to a population on the lower Volga around 4,200 years ago, which spread across Eurasia within a few centuries. The finding is often reported as identifying where horses were first tamed. It does not. Earlier populations elsewhere — at Botai in Kazakhstan a thousand years before — were kept, milked and harnessed, and left almost nothing in the genomes of the horses alive today. What the Volga lineage explains is not the beginning of horse-keeping but the replacement of every other kind.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"Horses kept at Botai were milked and harnessed a thousand years before the Volga population spread.","trap":"true-but-irrelevant"},{"letter":"B","content":"Modern domestic horses descend from a population that spread across Eurasia within a few centuries.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"C","content":"The genetic study identified the lower Volga as the place where horses were first tamed.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"D","content":"The genetic study explains why one lineage displaced the others, not where horse-keeping began."}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The text names the misreading in order to correct it. Choice C is the reading the passage explicitly rejects with “It does not,” and it is the most chosen answer because those words are the ones a skimmer sees.
  • A supporting detail is not the main idea. Botai is evidence for the correction, not the point of the passage.
  • True and incomplete. Choice B restates the genetic finding accurately and omits the argument the text is making about it.

Why A is wrong A supporting detail. Botai is introduced to show that horse-keeping predates the Volga lineage, and the passage's claim is about what the genetic result does and does not establish.

Why B is wrong This is the finding, correctly stated, with the argument stripped out. The text is about how that finding has been misread.

Why C is wrong The passage states the opposite in three words: “It does not.” This is the reported reading the text exists to correct.

Why D is right The final sentence gives the main idea directly: what the Volga lineage explains is not the beginning of horse-keeping but the replacement of every other kind.

stem_html:
Text 1

Fields left fallow recover nitrogen, and the medieval three-field rotation is often praised for recognizing this. But the rotation was not designed as soil science. It was a labor schedule: the fallow field was the one the village could not plough in time, and its rest was a consequence of how many oxen a village had, not a decision about nitrogen.

Text 2

Manorial accounts from the thirteenth century record fines for ploughing a field out of turn. A practice that was merely the residue of a labor shortage would not need to be enforced. Villages evidently understood that the rest itself mattered, whatever they believed was happening in the soil, and they policed it.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim about the fallow field in Text 1?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "By agreeing that the rotation had no basis in soil science but arguing that the fallow was nonetheless maintained deliberately."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "By arguing that medieval villages had a working theory of nitrogen fixation.", "trap": "too-extreme"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "By conceding that fines for ploughing out of turn were too rare to indicate a general practice.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "By pointing out that the number of oxen a village had varied more than Text 1 acknowledges.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two claims are bundled in Text 1 and only one is disputed. Text 2 leaves “not soil science” standing and attacks “not a decision.” A choice that rejects both, or neither, misreads the disagreement.
  • Overshooting the concession. Text 2 says villages understood that the rest itself mattered, whatever they believed was happening in the soil — which is a careful refusal to credit them with a theory. Choice B credits them with exactly the theory the sentence declines to.
  • Arguing against your own evidence. Choice C has Text 2 dismissing the fines, which are the whole of its case.

Why A is right Text 2's argument is that enforcement implies intent: a practice that was merely the residue of a labor shortage would not need to be enforced. That contradicts Text 1's “consequence, not a decision” while leaving its point about soil science untouched, and Text 2 explicitly brackets what villages believed about the soil.

Why B is wrong Text 2 goes out of its way not to claim this, saying only that villages understood the rest mattered whatever they believed was happening in the soil.

Why C is wrong The fines are Text 2's evidence. Conceding they were too rare to matter would leave its argument with nothing behind it.

Why D is wrong Text 2 never discusses oxen. Its case rests entirely on the manorial fines, and quibbling over the number of oxen would concede Text 1's framing.
